<!-- R1 of the repair batch of 2026-09-18, revised 2026-09-19 after the skeptic's refusal at 8b15d4af
     and the judge's ruling to repair at 513a9216 (JUDGE.md, SKEPTIC.md beside this file).
     Corrections made in that round are marked where they fall; the round's own work is the section
     "The regression this round removes, and how it was missed".  One line per paragraph. -->

# R1: a top-level mutable variable is outside the transaction

## What the rung repairs

`atomic do ... end` compiles on the bytecode path with a real transaction and a real retry loop (`CodeGen.forAtomicBlock`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1729-1757`, `startOver` at `:1753`), but a mutable variable declared at the top level of a component was read with a bare `GETSTATIC` and written with a bare `PUTSTATIC` on a non-final, non-volatile static field, so its reads and writes were not in the transaction at all.

That is one of two defects in the same code, and the second is not about concurrency: a write to such a variable from inside a nested code-generation context -- the body of a `for` loop, an arm of a parallel `do ... also do ... end` -- went to a *copy* of the value captured in the generated task's field, so the write was lost outright, at one thread as well as at four.

Both were landed by rung 3 (`4d419c9e8`) with `VarCodeGen.MutableStaticBinding`; before that rung, assignment to a top-level variable did not compile at all.

## What I inherited, and what I re-verified

The first launch of this batch died with its container 25 minutes in (`coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`, "How it is run"), and this branch already carried two commits: `029b7454` (two failing tests and a capture of their failure) and `c40d7f87` (the edit, with a capture of the pass).

I re-verified rather than trusted: I reverted the edited source files to the batch base `49ee5e91`, ran `ant compileAll`, wiped `default_repository/caches` and rebuilt it in library order, and re-ran the tests -- reproducing the failure (`probes/probe-runs-preedit.txt`, `probes/differential-preedit.txt`, and the pre-edit half of `probes/failure-before-edit.txt`); then restored the edit and repeated the whole cycle.

Two things did not survive that review, and both are in this rung's diff.

**The inherited concurrent test's own comment was wrong about the gate, and my correction of it was wrong in the other direction.** It had said that at the thread count "every gate target uses" the program passes whether or not the implementation is correct, citing the review's `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`; that pin is in the `testSystem` shards only (`build.xml:1184`), which run `SystemJUTest` and not `compiler_tests`. So far so good, and the chain I put in its place is right as far as it goes: the target that runs `compiler_tests` is `CompilerJUTest` under the `fastTrack` macro (`build.xml:927-953`), which sets `FORTRESS_CACHES` and no thread count and no `newenvironment`, so the forked JUnit JVM inhe
18:The first launch of this batch died with its container 25 minutes in (`coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`, "How it is run"), and this branch already carried two commits: `029b7454` (two failing tests and a capture of their failure) and `c40d7f87` (the edit, with a capture of the pass).
20:I re-verified rather than trusted: I reverted the edited source files to the batch base `49ee5e91`, ran `ant compileAll`, wiped `default_repository/caches` and rebuilt it in library order, and re-ran the tests -- reproducing the failure (`probes/probe-runs-preedit.txt`, `probes/differential-preedit.txt`, and the pre-edit half of `probes/failure-before-edit.txt`); then restored the edit and repeated the whole cycle.
24:**The inherited concurrent test's own comment was wrong about the gate, and my correction of it was wrong in the other direction.** It had said that at the thread count "every gate target uses" the program passes whether or not the implementation is correct, citing the review's `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`; that pin is in the `testSystem` shards only (`build.xml:1184`), which run `SystemJUTest` and not `compiler_tests`. So far so good, and the chain I put in its place is right as far as it goes: the target that runs `compiler_tests` is `CompilerJUTest` under the `fastTrack` macro (`build.xml:927-953`), which sets `FORTRESS_CACHES` and no thread count and no `newenvironment`, so the forked JUnit JVM inherits the shell; the harness runs each program in a further subprocess that inherits again (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/FileTests.java:480-486`); and `FortressExecutable.getNumThreads` falls back to the processor count or `floor(n/2)` (`:37-44`). What I missed is the first line of that method: the fallback applies **only when `FORTRESS_THREADS` is unset**, and `experiment/env.sh:6` exports `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, which the batch brief tells every agent to source and which `explorations/coordinator/iteration-cost.md:126` records as the setting of every run in the climb. In the gate as this project actually runs it there is one worker, and `AtomicTopLevelVar` passes vacuously there: measured on the base tree, `BASE run AtomicTopLevelVar THREADS=1 :: PASS` (`probes/skeptic/skeptic-basetree.txt`). I had to `unset FORTRESS_THREADS` in my own capture script (`tmp/final-capture.sh:40`) to get the rows I then called "the thread count the gate actually uses". The residual limitation is therefore not only a machine whose `availableProcessors` is 1 or 3; it is any shell that sourced the project's own env file. `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop` fails at one thread and is what carries the gate; the concurrent test is worth keeping as the check that the invariant holds under real contention, and the test's own comment now says all of this.
26:**The inherited deterministic test was racy and would have flaked in the gate.** Its loop body was a bare `inLoop := inLoop + 1` inside a *parallel* `for`, which is a data race by construction; once the repair let those writes reach the shared location, one run in nine gave 9 instead of 10 (`probes/capture-inherited-edit.txt`, `THREADS=default run=1`). The increment is now inside `atomic do ... end`, which is what `Specification/basic/memory-model.tex:69-75` requires of a program that wants a defined answer ("Updates to shared mutable locations must always be performed using an `atomic` expression"), and the expected values are then exact at any thread count.
32:`map/spec-to-implementation.md:176` places `atomic` for the compiled path at `CodeGen.forAtomicBlock:1729` via `forBlock`, with the runtime in `runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java`, and records that the block form compiles while `atomic <expr>` has no visitor and reaches `defaultCase`; both new tests use the block form, so the rung's construct is the one that compiles.
38:`map/test-coverage.md:185-186` says the fork-join runtime and the transactions are "barely" and "effectively no[t]" covered, and names the two reasons: every `testSystem` shard pins one thread, and `TransactionJUTest`'s multi-threaded half is commented out (`TestTask.java:43-44`). It says nothing about `compiler_tests`, and the line that should be added there is not the one I first wrote: that corpus does not pin a thread count of its own, so it runs at whatever the shell exported, and under `experiment/env.sh:6` that is one. The dark area is wider than the map records, not narrower.
60:`atomic.tex:96-107` is the chapter's own worked example and is the shape of the new test: a loop body that reads and writes a shared counter inside `atomic`, which "will appear to occur atomically with respect to all other threads -- including both other iterations of the loop body".
74:The cast after the read goes through `InstantiatingClassloader.generalizedCastTo` (`:352`) rather than a bare `CHECKCAST`, because the declared type may be a tuple or an arrow type, for which that helper emits a `castTo` call instead (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:2358-2395`); it is the same helper the surrounding `<clinit>` already uses for the same type name (`CodeGen.java:5891-5894`).
88:The inherited edit stored the value in the cell as a `runtimeValues.FValue`, which is an abstract *class* (`runtimeValues/FValue.java:13`), and that regressed a program that works on the base tree: a top-level mutable variable of arrow type. A compiled closure's class is not a subclass of `FValue`, so the verifier rejected the store -- `VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack ... 'P12Arrow$\=fn@8...' is not assignable to 'com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FValue'` (`probes/probe-types-postedit.txt`, against `probes/probe-types-preedit.txt` where the same program prints `f(1) = 3`).
90:The same store already existed for *local* mutable variables, so I probed that as the control: `probes/P15LocalArrow.fss` and `P16LocalArrowTask.fss` fail with the same `VerifyError` on the base tree (`probes/failure-before-edit.txt`). The cell's payload type was too narrow to hold a Fortress value, and the top-level case was not special.
92:The alternatives were: (a) widen the payload to the language's top type; (b) keep `FValue` and fall back to the old bare-`PUTSTATIC` representation for the types that do not fit, keeping two representations and leaving `atomic` silently non-transactional for a variable of arrow type; (c) leave the regression and record it. I took (a). It is the only one of the three that gives `atomic.tex:38-42` for every type of variable, it removes rather than adds a special case, and as a side effect it fixes the pre-existing defect for local mutable variables of arrow type. Its cost is that it changes two runtime signatures, so every compiled class that mentions them must be rebuilt -- which the cache wipe in the recipe already does -- and that the verifier no longer type-checks the payload, since assignability to an interface is not checked at verification time; the probes do that instead.
94:`fortress.AnyType.Any` rather than `java.lang.Object`: it is the type the language gives every value, `FValue` implements it (`FValue.java:13`), a generated arrow interface extends it (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:979-987`, directly when its parameters are all objects and transitively otherwise), and it says in the signature what the cell holds.
104:The alternative was to repair it in the same rung and accept that blast radius on the strength of a probe that no gated test covers. Against it: this rung's test needs the variable case; the field case needs its own test, and it needs the `final`-field distinction first, or it pays a cell for every immutable field in the language. It is a verified ledger row with a named fix, which is what rungs 6 and 7 did with row 317.
110:I kept the capture and made it capture the cell, because that is what the file's two right precedents do for the same construct and because excluding static bindings from the free-variable set would change the generated shape for *immutable* top-level variables too, which are captured by value today and are correct that way. The narrower change is the one that leaves immutable variables alone.
112:### 4. The gated test is the concurrent one, and no structural test was added
114:The brief allows a weaker structural check -- that the field carries `ACC_VOLATILE`, or that the read and write go through the transaction helpers -- if a genuinely concurrent test cannot be gated, and requires the limitation to be recorded either way.
116:A concurrent test can be *run* here and is worth having, but it cannot be relied on to fail in the gate: the count comes from the shell and `experiment/env.sh:6` pins it to 1 (the paragraph above). I still did not add a structural test, and the reason is now different from the one I first gave: the deterministic test `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop` fails on the base tree at one thread, so a gated failing test exists without asserting the shape of the fix, and this round adds a second one -- `AtomicTopLevelObjectVar`, which fails at one thread on the tree R1 landed. A structural check on `ACC_VOLATILE` would in fact have been wrong about this repair: the field is `ACC_FINAL` and the `volatile` is on the cell's payload (`MutableFValue.java:18`).
118:The residual limitation, recorded here and in the test's own comment: `AtomicTopLevelVar` discriminates only where the environment gives more than one worker, which the gate as this project runs it does not. Two deterministic tests carry the rung instead. Whether `fastTrack` should set a thread count for `compiler_tests` is a decision about the gate rather than about this rung -- its cost is nondeterminism across every compiled test program -- and it goes to Pavol in `record.md`.
120:### 5. The two `.test` files use a property the harness implements
122:Both inherited `.test` files asserted `run_out_WIcontains=PASS`. The harness implements six checks -- `_contains` (`FileTests.java:147`), `_does_not_contain` (`:155`), `_matches` (`:163`), `_WImatches` (`:171`), `_WCIequals` (`:180`) and `_equals` (`:190`) -- and does not implement `_WIcontains` at all, so that line is inert; the assertion that actually held was the default "stdout must contain pass or PASS" that applies when no check matched (`FileTests.java:266-272`). The three `.test` files this rung lands say `run_out_contains=PASS` and `run_out_does_not_contain=FAIL`, the form fifteen `.test` files already used on the base tree. My earlier count of five implemented checks and the range `:141-180` both stopped one check short of `_equals`.
124:Sixteen `.test` files carried the inert `run_out_WIcontains` on the base tree and sixteen still do (`git grep -l run_out_WIcontains 49ee5e91 -- 'ProjectFortress/**/*.test' | wc -l`, and the same at `HEAD`); eighteen was the count at this branch's inherited commit `029b7454`, before this rung's own two tests changed their form. Where the inert line is the only check those files still assert PASS through the default, so nothing is silently unchecked. I did not touch the sixteen: it is a record defect in the corpus, not this rung's subject, and it is offered as a record line in `record.md`.
126:Worth one sentence for the next brief: eight of those sixteen are the last climb's own new tests (`compiler_tests/MutableTopLevelVar.test` and `library_tests/EqualityRung1`, `HasRankRung2`, `AssertRung4`, `LineConcatRung5`, `IntLiteralRung6`, `IntLiteralArithRung7`, `BigSumRung8`), because the brief names `library_tests/Boolean.test` as the format to copy and that file carries the inert line. The brief is propagating it.
130:`probes/failure-before-edit.txt`, taken on the batch base `49ee5e91` with no source modification (`git diff 49ee5e91 -- ProjectFortress/src` empty), after `ant compileAll` and a wipe and library-order rebuild of `default_repository/caches`, with the two tests in the form this rung lands them in.
132:The key lines. The `THREADS=default` rows below are the rows my capture script produced by unsetting `FORTRESS_THREADS` (`tmp/final-capture.sh:40`), which gives two workers on this four-processor container; they are not the count the gate runs at under `experiment/env.sh`, which is one. Both tests also have `THREADS=1` rows in the same capture, and `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop` fails there too:
139:The same capture holds the pre-edit state of the three probes that bound the repair: `P12Arrow` prints `f(1) = 3` (a top-level mutable variable of arrow type *works* on the base tree, which is what made the inherited edit a regression), `P15LocalArrow` and `P16LocalArrowTask` fail with `VerifyError` (the same defect already present for local mutable variables), and `P10Field` gives 34481 of 40000 at four threads (the object-field defect this rung does not repair).
141:An earlier capture of the same failure for the earlier form of the tests is in commit `029b7454`; it was overwritten deliberately when the tests changed, because a recorded failure must be the failure of the test that lands.
147:`P12Arrow`, `P15LocalArrow` and `P16LocalArrowTask` all print `f(1) = 3`: the regression is gone and the pre-existing defect for local mutable variables of arrow type is gone with it. `P10Field` still gives 37831 of 40000 at four threads, unchanged, as the `MutableFieldVar` decision says it should.
151:**Every gated program that uses `atomic` on the compiled path**, before and after: `other_compiler_tests/atomic0` through `atomic6` and `nestedTransactions0` through `nestedTransactions2` -- ten programs, gated through `atomicTest.test` by `OtherCompilerJUTest`, whose `tests=` line names exactly those ten -- plus `nestedTransactions3.fss`, which exists in the same directory and is named by no `.test` file at all. Each was run at one and at four threads: 22 runs, of which 20 are gated programs and 2 are the ungated eleventh. All 22 PASS on the base tree, all 22 on the landed tree, and all 22 again after this round's guards (`probes/differential-preedit.txt`, `probes/differential-final.txt`, `probes/differential-after-guard.txt`; `-any.txt` is the same set on the intermediate state). These programs exercise `LocalMutableVar` and `MutableTaskVarCodeGen`, whose emitted descriptors this rung changed, so they are the check on the payload-type edit.
153:**The interpreter, as evidence rather than oracle** (`probes/walk-differential.txt`): under `walk`, at one thread and at four, `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop` and `AtomicTopLevelVar` both print PASS. So the unrepaired compiled path diverged from the interpreter on both tests, the specification settles that divergence against the compiled run (`atomic.tex:38-42`, `bindings.tex:57-59`), and the repair removes it.
157:**The type probes** (`probes/probe-types-preedit.txt` on the base tree, `-final.txt` on the landed one): a top-level mutable variable of an object type, of arrow type and of type `String`, and a local mutable variable of an object type, with the two local arrow probes added once the payload question appeared. The arrow cases are the interesting ones and are discussed above; the rest are unchanged.
167:The subset is every program in `ProjectFortress/tests/` that declares a variable at the top level of a component: I re-derived it with a column-anchored grep and it is exactly the inherited twenty -- nineteen matched by `^var` or `^name: T :=`, plus `XXXmutableTopVarWithoutType.fss`, whose `var (x, y) = (1, 2)` my expression missed and which `forVarDeclPrePass` rejects as a tupled left-hand side either way.
169:Two different greps are easy to confuse here and both matter. The one above derives the *ladder subset* -- gated programs that declare a top-level variable -- and my skeptic rightly extended it: `compiler_tests` holds three more such programs (rung 3's `MutableTopLevelVar.fss`, and `Compiled5.p.fss:15` `var x: ZZ32 = 3` and `Compiled9.b.fss:34` `var A: String = "A string"`), of which the last two are named only by `AfterTypeChecking.test` and `AfterDisambiguate.test`, whose `tests=` lines run `typecheck` and `disambiguate` and stop there, so no code-generation change reaches them; `other_compiler_tests` and `library_tests` hold none and `not_passing_yet` holds two and is ungated. The other grep is the batch's step 6 -- a competing declaration of every *name* this rung adds -- and this round ran it over all five corpora for `counter`, `iterations`, `bump`, `inLoop`, `inArmA`, `inArmB`, `Box` and the three component names. Two files declare one of those names at the top level of their own component (`tests/GS2.fss:16` `counter:ZZ32 := 0`, `library_tests/AssertRung4.fss:48` `bump(n: ZZ32): ZZ32`), and neither can collide: every name this rung adds is inside a `compiler_tests` component and none is exported through an api, which is what made rung 1's `trait Equality` collision possible. `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4348` does declare a generic `object Box[\T\](var val: T)`, but that is the interpreter's library, the compiled path imports `CompilerBuiltin`/`CompilerLibrary`, which declare no `Box`, and `AtomicTopLevelObjectVar` prints `PASS` under `walk` as well, so the two declarations coexist there too.
173:The first run of the subset on the repaired tree differed from that baseline in exactly one file, and it was a regression: `tests/InitOrderWithMutable.fss` compiled but its run exited 1 with
182:This is legitimate under the specification rather than a convenience, and the citation I first gave was the weaker of the two available. The prescriptive one is `Specification/basic/variables.tex:122-123`: "The initializer expressions of top-level variable declarations can refer to variables declared later in textual order." `Specification/basic/components/initialization.tex:15-17,29-30` is the *procedure* -- all top-level variables and singleton object fields are initialized "before their use", in no prescribed textual order -- so it declines to forbid a forward reference rather than licensing one. `variables.tex:122-123` licenses it outright, and `tests/InitOrderWithMutable.fss` is the team's own test of exactly that, which is how the regression was caught.
192:`atomic` used as an expression -- `atomic x := 1` rather than `atomic do x := 1 end` -- still has no visitor in `CodeGen` and reaches `defaultCase` (`map/spec-to-implementation.md:176`). Both new tests use the block form for that reason. `compiler_tests/Compiled170.fss`, which the inherited test comment cited as its model, is one of the programs that cannot compile for this reason and is in no `.test` file; the citation is gone.
202:The chain, which I re-read frame by frame rather than taking from the refusal. `Transaction.TXWrite` built its debug message by concatenation before testing the flag (`runtimeSystem/Transaction.java:227`; the flag is `private static boolean debug = false` at `:30` and `debug(String)` tests it only at `:56-58`, after Java has already built the argument). Concatenating the payload calls `MutableFValue.toString` (`runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java:38-40`), which renders the value, which for a compiled user object is `FValue.toString` (`runtimeValues/FValue.java:25-27`) -- `this.asString().toString()` -- and `trait Object`'s default `asString` is `jAsString(self)` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:338`), bound to `stringOps.asString` (`:270`), which returns `a.toString()` (`nativeHelpers/stringOps.java:38-40`). That is a three-frame cycle with no base case. `probes/skeptic/sk25-recursion-entry.txt` has the frames; 4,391 of them.
214:**All fourteen sites of `Transaction.java`, not the nine that can crash.** Nine stringify a Fortress value or a table of them (`:162, :166, :185, :203, :227, :232, :249, :265, :274`) and are the entries into the cycle; `:232` renders both hash tables whole. The other five build a string of an `int` or a constant on every abort, begin, validate and failed commit. One rule for the file is verified with one `grep` and leaves no later reader to work out which sites are safe. The alternative was the nine alone, the narrowest diff; I rejected it because the narrower diff is the one that needs a comment to explain itself.
220:**The case is gated, not only probed.** `compiler_tests/AtomicTopLevelObjectVar` is a new program: `object Box(n: ZZ32) end` with no `asString` of its own, a top-level `b: Box := Box(1)` and a local `var c: Box = Box(1)`, each assigned inside its own `atomic` block and read after. The alternative was to leave `SK25` as a probe, which no gate runs. The top-level half of this program also passes on `49ee5e91` -- that is the point: the state it guards against is the tree R1 landed. Its local half most likely fails on `49ee5e91` as well, but that is an inference and not a measurement: `SK20LocalTrait`, which was run on the base tree and overflows there, is a *trait*-typed local variable, while this test's `var c: Box` is object-typed and this program has never been run on the base tree; the inference is from that probe together with `LocalMutableVar`'s having always routed through `TXWrite`. The test's recorded failure is against the pre-guard landed tree and does not rest on the claim.
226:`probes/pass-after-guard.txt`: after `ant compileAll` (`tmp/compileAll-guard.log`, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`), a wipe of `default_repository/caches` and the library-order rebuild (`tmp/cache-rebuild-guard.log`: `AnyType` 19 s, `CompilerBuiltin` 103 s, `CompilerLibrary` 17 s, `CompilerAlgebra` 2 s, `CompilerSystem` 1 s), all four `compiler_tests` programs -- `AtomicTopLevelObjectVar`, `AtomicTopLevelVar`, `MutableTopLevelVarInLoop` and rung 3's `MutableTopLevelVar` -- at `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, unset and `=4`, with three runs each for the concurrent one: 18 runs, every one `PASS`. `AtomicTopLevelObjectVar` also prints `PASS` under `walk`.
234:`probes/differential-after-guard.txt`: the ten programs `atomicTest.test` names plus `nestedTransactions3`, at one and at four threads, 22 of 22 `PASS`, identical row for row to `differential-final.txt`.

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full stop
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md; exactly one must, else the
                         nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
usage: ledger.py [-h] COMMAND ...

The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

positional arguments:
  COMMAND

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored

content.content:
23:> The compiled world's mutable-variable cell holds `fortress.AnyType.Any`, the language's top type, not `runtimeValues.FValue`: `FValue` is an abstract class (`runtimeValues/FValue.java:13`) and a compiled closure is not one of its subclasses, so a mutable variable of arrow type failed the verifier. The defect was already in the tree for *local* mutable variables, which have always been stored in such a cell (`compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/probes/P15LocalArrow.fss`, `P16LocalArrowTask.fss`: `VerifyError` on `49ee5e91`, `f(1) = 3` after R1), and R1 fixed both kinds by widening the payload (`runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java:18-32`, `runtimeSystem/Transaction.java:20,27-28,144,152,226`).
53:> | 323 | **`walk` rejects a singleton object's field initializer that reads a top-level *mutable* variable declared later in the component**, which the compiled path runs correctly: `ProgramError: Attempt to find type of uninitialized variable: thunk (IntLiteralExpr …)` at the field's own line, while the compiled path prints the right answers on the base tree and the repaired one alike. The reference is licensed by the specification, so this is a defect of the interpreter. Narrowed by one control: with the later variable *immutable* (`d: ZZ32 = 5` in place of `d: ZZ32 := 5`) `walk` accepts the same program, and `tests/InitOrderWithMutable.fss` shows `walk` accepts a *top-level* initializer reading a later mutable variable — so the failure is specific to a singleton object field initializer reading a later mutable variable. | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (walk interpreter) | `basic/variables.tex:122-123` — "The initializer expressions of top-level variable declarations can refer to variables declared later in textual order" — with `basic/components/initialization.tex:15-17,29-30` (top-level variables and singleton object fields are initialized before their use, in no prescribed textual order) and `basic/objects.tex:202-203` (singleton initialization is nondeterministic) | `compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/probes/skeptic/SK5InitFwd.fss` and `SK26InitFwdImmutable.fss` (the control); captures in `skeptic-differential-after-guard.txt` and `sk26-initfwd-immutable.txt` | ours | Compiled, both trees: `a = 11 b = 10 c = 12 Holder.f = 5 d = 5`. The rung's own pre-pass fix (`CodeGen.addTopLevelVarBinding`) is what makes the compiled side right for the *variable* case; the object-field case was already right there. |

content.content:
**`asZZ32` left alone.**  For a string-carried numeral it is correct only by accident:
`smallerVal` holds `BOGUS`, which falls outside `int` range, so the check refuses it.
Adding `largerVal == null` would change no behaviour today and was left out to keep the
diff to what the tests need; the dependency on the sentinel's value is recorded here.

**The test's expected values are computed, not written twice.**  Every expectation in
`compiler_tests/IntLiteralWrapRepairR2.fss` is built at run time from numerals of bit length
16, 17, 31, 33 and 63, none of which any branch of the split ever mis-read, following
`library_tests/IntLiteralArithRung7.fss:39-43`.  A literal `4294967295` on the expected side
would have wrapped identically and the test would have passed before the repair.

**The test is in `compiler_tests/`, not `library_tests/`.**  `PLAN.md` step 1 of the order of
work puts codegen rungs there, and `CompilerJUTest.java:36,42` sweeps that directory in
`testFast` (`build.xml:965`).

## The failure-mode question

**One loud failure becomes a quiet value, and this report first did not say so.**
`FIntLiteral.asNN64`'s pre-image was `if (largerVal == null) return
FNN64.make((long)smallerVal); throw outOfRange("NN64");` -- it threw for *every*
string-carried numeral -- and `simpleIntLiteralArith.fromBigInteger` sends every `IntLiteral`
arithmetic result of bit length 64 or more to the string branch (`:31-32`), a path this rung
does not touch.  So the transition is reachable without a numeral of bit length 64 anywhere
in the source.  The skeptic's probe `probes/skeptic/s3.fss` is the case: `x =
9223372036854775807` then `n: NN64 = x + x + 1` raised `Error: Not in range for NN64:
18446744073709551615` before this rung and now computes the value, which
`probes/skeptic/s3.compiled` shows **rendered as `-1`**.

The value is the specification-correct one -- `literals.tex:83-86` gives the numeral its

(************************************************************
* Numeric hierarchy
************************************************************)

(** Place holder for exclusions of AdditiveGroup **)
trait AnyAdditiveGroup end

(** Additive group making use of +.  Must define + and either unary or binary -. **)
trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends AnyAdditiveGroup
    getter zero(): T = self - self
    opr +(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self, other: T): T = self + (-other)
    opr -(self) : T = self.zero - self
end

(** Place holder for exclusions of MultiplicativeRing **)
trait AnyMultiplicativeRing end

(** Multiplicative ring using TIMES and juxtaposition.
    Define opr TIMES; juxtaposition is defined in terms of TIMES. **)
trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
        extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    getter one(): T
    opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
    opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T = self TIMES other

228:As discussed in \secref{type-relations},
229:the exclusion relation is symmetric.
230:Thus, if \VAR{T} excludes \VAR{U}

235:If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
236:then every type listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause extends \VAR{T},
237:and every value of type \VAR{T} is a value of one of the listed types.
238:A listed type may be an instantiation of a parameterized trait,
239:provided that every static variable that occurs in its static arguments
240:is a static parameter of \VAR{T}
241:or a \KWD{where}-clause variable of the declaration of \VAR{T}
242:(\secref{where-clauses}),
243:which the listed type then holds at every value of:
244:a trait declared
245:\EXP{\KWD{trait}\;\TYP{NatParam}\;\KWD{comprises}\;\{N\llbracket{}n\rrbracket\}\;\KWD{where}\;\llbracket\KWD{nat}\;n\rrbracket}
246:lists \EXP{N\llbracket{}n\rrbracket} at every \KWD{nat} value of \VAR{n}.
247:A trait or object that explicitly extends \VAR{T}
248:must be a subtype of a listed type,
249:unless it is a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause of its own
250:each of whose listed types meets this requirement,
251:or a trait with static parameters
252:such that at least one trait or object extends it
253:and every trait or object that extends it
254:is a subtype of a listed type.
255:If \VAR{T} has static parameters,
256:these statements hold of each instantiation of \VAR{T},
257:with the static parameters of \VAR{T} in the listed types
258:replaced by the corresponding static arguments.
259:\revision{revival-comprises}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said here,
260:in a draft note, that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause
261:are exactly the traits that immediately extend \VAR{T}
262:and that each of them must list \VAR{T} in its \KWD{extends} clause.
263:The revival states the reading of the team's later Types chapter
264:(Luchangco, 2012) and of the type group's calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012):
265:the clause says to which types the values of \VAR{T} belong.
266:A parameterized trait with a static parameter that \VAR{T} does not have

268:it may stand unlisted between \VAR{T} and the listed types,

272:This also answers the third question of the draft note on trait identifiers above,

70:## How `XXX` works
72:- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
73:- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
75:- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
76:- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.

A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.

49:- **The bit identities three of the library sites use.** For a power of two `p`, `p - 1` is the mask of the bits below `p`, and `-p` is the mask of the bits at and above it. For positive `p` both are ordinary integers that fit. When `p` is the sign bit alone, which as a number is the minimum, the true values of `p - 1` and `-p` do not fit, but their wrapped values, the maximum and the minimum, are exactly the masks wanted. Those sites are right *because* the machine wraps: they are modular arithmetic spelled with the ordinary operators.
53:- **`walk`, `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`.** The natives are one-line Java arithmetic that wraps (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:98-125` and `Long.java`'s twins; the wrapped values are measured in row 379). Since rung I, `GCD` and `LCM` check (`Int.java:137`, `:145`). `partitionL`, the largest power of two below its argument, is the native `Integer.highestOneBit(u - 1)` (`Int.java:212-216`), whose `u - 1` wraps inside Java whatever the Fortress operators do.
117:- 2007-08-24, Sukyoung Ryu, `0370a14b2`: the team's draft api `StandardLibrary/Fortress.Number.fsi` makes `ZZ` a ring under `DOTPLUS`, `DOTMINUS`, `DOTTIMES` and declares the operators (today `Library/incomplete/basic/Fortress.Number.fsi:87-89`, `:110-125`); the Fortify typesetter maps `DOTPLUS` to ∔ in the same tree.
131:- `LinearCongruential` and the Mersenne twister: `7d3df35e8`, 2010-06-21, senokay (identity unresolved, `research/authorship.md:67`).
156:- **(d) `LinearCongruential`**, `Library/Random.fss:235` (measured) and `:241` (by reading). It means arithmetic modulo 2^48, done through arithmetic modulo 2^64. It becomes `((mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add) MOD modulus`: the same values, no cost, `MOD` bringing a negative wrapped value back into range as it does today. This is right only because 2^48 divides 2^64. The object is generic in its modulus (`Random.fss:222`) and built once, with 2^48 (`:253`); for a modulus that is not a power of two, today's code and this one both give wrong numbers without a word (section 11). Alternatives: exact through `ZZ`, right for every modulus, at a `BigInteger` per random number (`QuickCheckTest` alone meets 146K overflowing products); or the Mersenne twister's habit (way 1), splitting the state into 24-bit halves so every product fits, about five lines and three multiplications.
188:- **`LinearCongruential` is wrong for most moduli.** The object is generic in its modulus, but wrapping modulo 2^64 and then taking `MOD modulus` is right only when the modulus is a power of two; the library builds it only with 2^48 (`Library/Random.fss:222`, `:253`).

\section{Coercion Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.
A declaration with static parameters is applicable, without or with coercion,
when some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is, and
declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare
(\secref{functional-applicability}, \secref{resolving-overloading}); the
declaration selected is then instantiated as \secref{static-arg-inference}
describes, with the rule for a numeral whose conversions tie
(\secref{numeral-default}).

- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. failure was wrong.  The cost is nonetheless real and is the reason this belongs with the
rendering row rather than beside it: the error that *named* the true value is gone, and what
replaces it prints as `-1`, because `FNN64.toString` is signed (`runtimeValues/FNN64.java:20`).
That is ledger row 326, and the two facts are one situation.  `walk` has no counterpart: it
refuses the coercion outright (`probes/skeptic/s3.walk`, "RHS expression type Long is not
assignable to LHS type NN64").

In the other direction -- a quiet wrong value becoming a loud failure -- there are four:
`asZZ32`, `asZZ64` and `asNN32` now raise `Not in range for ...` where they silently
truncated, which row 325 records for annotated declarations; `asNN32` on a string-carried
numeral now raises where it returned the `BOGUS` sentinel's low half
(`probes/skeptic/s2`); and `p37`'s comparison, row 328.

| `r2b` `NN32`/`NN64` rendering | walk refuses the coercion; compiled prints `-1` for both | unchanged | not settled by this rung's reading; a ledger row is owed, see below |
| `r2c`, `r2d`, `r2f` out-of-range coercions | walk refuses; compiled silently truncates | walk refuses; compiled raises `Not in range for ...` | the paths now agree in outcome and differ only in whether the diagnostic is static or dynamic; recorded, not repaired |
| `p37` comparison of a numeral of bit length 64 | walk three `false` lines; compiled `true` | walk unchanged; compiled raises `Not in range for ZZ64: 18446744073709551615` | `literals.tex:83-86`: against the compiled run both before and after -- a quiet wrong answer became a loud one, and the comparison site is ledger row 328, outside this rung |

40:- **The unsigned types.** The specification's overflow rule covers every integer result (`opr-overview.tex:155`), so `NN32` and `NN64` do not wrap by design. Under `walk` they wrap today: their natives call `com.naturalbridge.misc.Unsigned.add`, which is a bare `iadd` (read with `javap` from `ProjectFortress/third_party/unsigned/unsigned.jar`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/NN32.java:109-112`). Row 379 does not cover them (section 11).
133:- Outside the eleven: `UnsignedTest`'s use of unary `-` on an unsigned value as 2^w minus a number, `dc41d5000`, 2008-07-21, Steele (section 11).
156:- **(d) `LinearCongruential`**, `Library/Random.fss:235` (measured) and `:241` (by reading). It means arithmetic modulo 2^48, done through arithmetic modulo 2^64. It becomes `((mult DOTTIMES widen(state)) DOTPLUS add) MOD modulus`: the same values, no cost, `MOD` bringing a negative wrapped value back into range as it does today. This is right only because 2^48 divides 2^64. The object is generic in its modulus (`Random.fss:222`) and built once, with 2^48 (`:253`); for a modulus that is not a power of two, today's code and this one both give wrong numbers without a word (section 11). Alternatives: exact through `ZZ`, right for every modulus, at a `BigInteger` per random number (`QuickCheckTest` alone meets 146K overflowing products); or the Mersenne twister's habit (way 1), splitting the state into 24-bit halves so every product fits, about five lines and three multiplications.
## 11. Found on the way

- **A sixth split site.** `Library/RangeInternals.fss:1265-1266` has the same `split-1` and the same distance as the five that row 403 and rung O's report list (by reading).
- **The unsigned types wrap under `walk` and row 379 does not cover them.** `NN32` and `NN64` arithmetic goes through `com.naturalbridge.misc.Unsigned.add`, `subtract` and `multiplyTo…`, which are bare `iadd` and `lmul` (read with `javap`; `NN32.java:103-124`, `UnsignedLong.java:104-125`), while t
- **`LinearCongruential` is wrong for most moduli.** The object is generic in its modulus, but wrapping modulo 2^64 and then taking `MOD modulus` is right only when the modulus is a power of two; the library builds it only with 2^48 (`Library/Random.fss:222`, `:253`).
- **A wrapping operator under `walk` needs natives of its own.** Rung O's patch changes today's ten natives in place (`REPORT.md` § 3), so after it no native wraps; a wrapping operator bound to the old names would start to throw.
- **The box family means "toward zero" on both kinds of number.** Saturation clamps toward zero, and the same boxed operators on floats round toward zero (`opr-overview.tex:181`, `:214`). That is a design reason behind the specification's pairing, relevant to row 348.

No gated test runs a mutable variable of arrow type compiled; the cell's gated tests are `compiler_tests/MutableTopLevelVarInLoop`, `AtomicTopLevelVar` and `AtomicTopLevelObjectVar`.
- **A numeral's value reaches the compiled world intact** (`compile-ladder/repair-r2-literal-wrap/REPORT.md`; row 317). `CodeGen.forIntLiteralExpr` chooses a numeral's representation by `BigInteger.bitLength()` `<= 31` and `<= 63`, exact for both signs (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3889-3923`), and `FIntLiteral.asNN64` reads the decimal string a numeral of bit length 64 keeps (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:85-95`), so `4294967295` and `18446744073709551615` keep their values (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-86`) and the compiled run agrees with `walk`. Gated by `compiler_tests/IntLiteralWrapRepairR2`. An `IntLiteral` arithmetic result of bit length 64 or more is carried as its decimal string too (`nativeHelpers/simpleIntLiteralArith.java:19-22`), so `n: NN64 = x + x + 1` for `x = 9223372036854775807` holds 2^64-1, the correct value, and prints `-1`, because `FNN64.toString` is signed (`compiler/runtimeValues/FNN64.java:20`; row 326, open); `walk` refuses that coercion (REPORT, "The failure-mode question").
